title: Config parameters
description: Every server configuration parameter. Context says when a change takes effect: **postmaster** = server restart, **sighup** = config reload, **superuser** = privileged SET, **user** = any session SET, **backend** / **superuser-backend** = fixed at connection start, **internal** = read-only. **also per table** = can be overridden for one table with a storage parameter; **build option** = exists only in a server compiled with the named macro.
rows: Additional PID file for admin programs

Comma-separated host names/IPs to listen on. `*` = all interfaces, `0.0.0.0` = all IPv4, `::` = all IPv6; empty = no TCP at all (Unix sockets only). Server starts if at least one address can be opened (warning for others).
TCP port, same for all addresses.
typically 100 (may be less, determined by initdb from kernel settings)
Max concurrent connections. Sizes shared-memory resources. Standby must have >= primary's value or queries are not allowed on the standby.

Slots reserved for roles with privileges of `pg_use_reserved_connections`. When free slots > superuser_reserved_connections but <= superuser_reserved_connections + reserved_connections, only superusers and those roles are accepted. Must be < max_connections - superuser_reserved_connections.
Slots reserved for superusers: when active connections >= max_connections - this, only superusers accepted. Final emergency reserve. Must be < max_connections - reserved_connections.

Comma-separated directories for Unix-domain sockets; empty = none. Value starting with `@` = Linux abstract-namespace socket (convention `@/tmp`). Socket file `.s.PGSQL.nnnn` (nnnn = port) plus ordinary lock file `.s.PGSQL.nnnn.lock`; never remove manually.
Owning group of socket. Ignored on Windows and for abstract sockets.
Socket permissions; only write permission matters. Alternatives 0770, 0700. Ignored on Solaris 10 and abstract sockets. Independent of pg_hba.conf.
Idle time before OS sends TCP keepalive. Needs TCP_KEEPIDLE; ignored (reads 0) on Unix sockets.
Lost keepalives before connection is considered dead (TCP_KEEPCNT; not Windows).
Time transmitted data may stay unacknowledged before connection is forcibly closed (TCP_USER_TIMEOUT; not Windows).

Interval between polls of the socket while running a query, so long queries abort sooner if the client is gone. Linux, macOS, illumos, BSDs only. Without it loss is detected only at next socket interaction.
Max time to complete client authentication, else server closes connection.
Algorithm for passwords set in CREATE/ALTER ROLE: `scram-sha-256` or `md5` (MD5 deprecated, to be removed).
SCRAM-SHA-256 iteration count; fixed at encryption time (existing passwords unaffected). Caveat: differing iteration counts let an unauthenticated user discern role existence.
WARNING when CREATE/ALTER ROLE sets an MD5 password.
Kerberos key file; empty => system default.
Accept GSSAPI credentials delegated from client.
Library/libraries validating OAuth tokens. If exactly one, used by default; otherwise every `oauth` HBA entry must set `validator`. No validator ships with PostgreSQL.
Trusted CA file; relative to data directory.
Client certificate revocation list file (loaded at start/reload).
CRL directory (prepare with `openssl rehash`/`c_rehash`); loaded on demand at connection time, new CRLs used immediately.

Ciphers for TLS <= 1.2. HIGH (AES, Camellia, 3DES), MEDIUM (RC4, SEED), `+3DES` reorders 3DES after other HIGH/MEDIUM, `!aNULL` disables anonymous suites (MITM-vulnerable). `openssl ciphers -v '...'` to inspect.
Named group(s) for TLS key exchange, colon-separated. **Before 18.0 named `ssl_ecdh_curve` and accepted a single value.**
TLSv1, TLSv1.1, TLSv1.2, TLSv1.3; SSLv2/v3 always disabled.
External command printing passphrase on stdout, exit 0; `%p` = prompt string, `%%` literal.
Whether the passphrase command is also called during reload; if off, SSL config is not reloaded when a passphrase is needed. Must be on for Windows.
typically 128MB (less if kernel cannot support, per initdb)

Shared memory buffers. Minimum 128 kB. Starting point on a dedicated server with >= 1GB RAM: **25% of RAM**; more than **40% of RAM** unlikely to help because PostgreSQL also relies on the OS cache. Larger values usually need larger `max_wal_size`.

`try` / `on` (fail to start if unavailable) / `off`. Main shared memory area only. Linux (only with shared_memory_type=mmap) and Windows ("large pages", needs "Lock pages in memory" right). Actual state in `huge_pages_status`. Transparent huge pages (THP) are discouraged.
Huge page size; non-default only on Linux. Common: 2MB & 1GB (Intel/AMD), 16MB & 16GB (POWER), 64kB/2MB/32MB/1GB (ARM).
user (only before first use of temp tables in the session)
Max session-local buffers for temporary tables. Cost of an unused increment: a buffer descriptor, about **64 bytes**; a used buffer costs an additional 8192 bytes (BLCKSZ).
Max simultaneously "prepared" transactions (PREPARE TRANSACTION). If used, set >= max_connections. Standby must be >= primary.

**Base max memory per query operation (sort or hash table) before spilling to temporary disk files.** Each sort/hash node in a plan, in each session (and each parallel worker), may use this much. Sorts: ORDER BY, DISTINCT, merge joins. Hash tables: hash joins, hash aggregation, memoize nodes, hash-based IN subqueries.
Hash-operation memory limit = work_mem * hash_mem_multiplier. 2.0-8.0 or more may help when work_mem is already >= 40MB.
Max memory for maintenance: VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY. Autovacuum may allocate up to autovacuum_max_workers times this.

Size of the Buffer Access Strategy ring used by VACUUM and ANALYZE. 0 = may use any number of shared buffers; otherwise 128 kB to 16 GB; silently capped at 1/8 of shared_buffers. Overridable per command with `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`.
Max memory for logical decoding before decoded changes spill to local disk; one buffer per replication connection.
0 => shared_buffers/512, up to 1024 blocks, not fewer than 16 blocks
Max safe execution stack depth; ideal = kernel `ulimit -s` minus ~1 MB safety margin (depth is only checked in key potentially-recursive routines). Too high => runaway recursion can crash a backend.
Implementation for the main shared memory region: `mmap` (anonymous shared memory via mmap), `sysv` (shmget; not default anywhere, discouraged), `windows`.
DSM implementation: `posix` (shm_open), `sysv` (shmget), `windows`, `mmap` (memory-mapped files in data directory `pg_dynshmem`; discouraged, never default).
Memory preallocated at startup for parallel queries; affected by huge_pages. When exhausted, parallel queries allocate DSM from the OS via dynamic_shared_memory_type.
Max disk space a process may use for temporary files (sort/hash temp files, held-cursor storage) at any instant; exceeding cancels the transaction. Explicit temporary tables do NOT count.
`COPY` or `CLONE` (copy_file_range() on Linux/FreeBSD, copyfile on macOS). Affects `CREATE DATABASE ... STRATEGY=FILE_COPY` and `ALTER DATABASE ... SET TABLESPACE`.

How data files are extended in bulk operations such as COPY. posix_fallocate silently falls back to write_zeros if FS lacks support; BTRFS disables compression with it. `write_zeros` always used when extending by 8 blocks or fewer.
Max pages for the NOTIFY/LISTEN queue (8 GB of disk at 8 kB pages).
Max files each server subprocess may open simultaneously (files already open in postmaster not counted). Reduce on "Too many open files".
Sleep between rounds; longer sleep when no dirty buffers. Effective resolution may be 10 ms.
Max buffers written per round; 0 disables background writing (checkpoints unaffected).
Next-round need estimate = recent average buffer need * multiplier; write dirty buffers until that many clean reusable buffers exist (capped by lru_maxpages). 1.0 = "just in time".
After this much written by bgwriter, force OS writeback. Range 0 (disabled) to 2MB.
After this much written by one backend, force OS writeback. Range 0-2MB.

Number of concurrent storage I/O operations expected; range 1-1000, 0 disables asynchronous I/O requests. Also controls prefetch distance on systems with prefetch advice. Overridable per tablespace (ALTER TABLESPACE).
Same, for maintenance work done on behalf of many sessions; per-tablespace override.
Hard cap on combined-I/O size; silently limits `io_combine_limit`. Max typically 1MB on Unix, 128kB on Windows.
Largest I/O size in operations that combine I/O.
-1 (auto from shared_buffers and max processes: max_connections, autovacuum_worker_slots, max_worker_processes, max_wal_senders; not more than 64)
Max I/O operations one process can execute simultaneously.
**Asynchronous I/O method (PG 18):** `worker` (I/O worker processes), `io_uring` (needs `--with-liburing`), `sync` (execute AIO-eligible I/O synchronously).
Number of I/O worker processes (only with io_method=worker).
Max background processes the cluster supports. Standby must be >= primary.

Max workers started by one Gather / Gather Merge node; 0 disables parallel query. Workers come from max_worker_processes pool, limited by max_parallel_workers; may get fewer at run time. work_mem applies per worker: 4 workers => up to 5x the resources.

Max parallel workers for one utility command: CREATE INDEX for **B-tree, GIN, or BRIN**, and VACUUM without FULL. 0 disables. maintenance_work_mem is a limit for the entire utility command regardless of worker count.
Max workers for parallel operations cluster-wide; values above max_worker_processes have no effect.
Leader also executes the plan under Gather/Gather Merge instead of only waiting for workers.

How much information goes to WAL: `minimal` (only crash/immediate-shutdown recovery info) < `replica` (archiving + replication + read-only standby queries) < `logical` (adds logical decoding info). Each level includes lower ones. Old values `archive` and `hot_standby` (pre-9.6) map to `replica`.

Force updates physically to disk via fsync() or equivalent (see wal_sync_method). Off => risk of unrecoverable corruption after OS/hardware crash. If turned off also consider turning off full_page_writes.
How much WAL processing must complete before "success" is returned: `remote_apply`, `on`, `remote_write`, `local`, `off`.
first supported in list order, except `fdatasync` on Linux and FreeBSD

`open_datasync` (open() O_DSYNC), `fdatasync` (fdatasync() at each commit), `fsync`, `fsync_writethrough` (fsync forcing write-through of disk write cache), `open_sync` (O_SYNC). Irrelevant if fsync is off.
Write entire page content to WAL on the first modification of that page after a checkpoint (torn-page protection).

Also write full page on first post-checkpoint modification even for hint-bit-only changes. Ignored (always logged) when data checksums are enabled. Useful to measure the extra WAL checksums would cause.
Compress full page images in WAL: `pglz`, `lz4` (--with-lz4), `zstd` (--with-zstd); `on` = historical spelling of pglz.
Zero-fill new WAL files (ensures space allocated). Off: only the final byte is written (useful on COW file systems).
Recycle WAL files by renaming instead of creating new ones (off may be faster on COW file systems).
-1 => **1/32nd (about 3%) of shared_buffers, not less than 64kB nor more than one WAL segment (typically 16MB)**
Shared memory for WAL not yet written to disk. Positive values below 32kB are treated as 32kB. WAL buffers are written out at every transaction commit.
How often WAL writer flushes WAL (time). After a flush it sleeps this long unless woken by an asynchronously committing transaction.
Flush by volume: if last flush < wal_writer_delay ago AND < this much WAL produced since, WAL is only written to OS, not flushed. 0 => always flush immediately.
With wal_level=minimal, at commit after creating/rewriting a permanent relation: data smaller than this is written to WAL; otherwise the affected files are fsynced.

Delay before a WAL flush is initiated (group commit). Only applied if at least `commit_siblings` other transactions are active; never if fsync is off. Since 9.3: first process ready to flush waits the interval, later ones wait only until the leader finishes.
Min concurrent open transactions required to perform the commit_delay.
Max time between automatic WAL checkpoints. Range 30 seconds to one day. Larger => longer crash recovery.
Target for checkpoint completion as a fraction of the time between checkpoints; spreads I/O. Reducing not recommended.
Force OS writeback after this much checkpoint data written. Range 0-2MB.
Log a message if checkpoints caused by WAL segment filling occur closer together than this (suggests raising max_wal_size). 0 disables; none if checkpoint_timeout < checkpoint_warning.
Max WAL size to allow between automatic checkpoints; **soft limit** (exceeded under heavy load, failing archive_command/archive_library, high wal_keep_size).
While WAL usage stays below this, old WAL files are always recycled at checkpoint rather than removed.
`off`, `on`, `always` (archiver also runs during archive recovery/standby; restored or streamed files are archived again). Cannot be enabled with wal_level=minimal.

Shell command to archive a completed WAL segment; `%p` = path of file (relative to data directory), `%f` = file name, `%%` = literal. Must return zero only on success. Empty while archive_mode on => archiving temporarily disabled, WAL accumulates. Error if both archive_command and archive_library set. `/bin/true` effectively disables archiving but breaks the WAL chain.
Shared library for archiving; empty => shell archive_command. Archiver process restarted by postmaster on change.

Force a WAL segment switch after this much time since the last switch if there was any activity (including a single checkpoint). Early-closed files are still full length (bloats archive); a minute or so is reasonable.

Prefetch blocks referenced in WAL that are not yet in the buffer pool during recovery: `off`, `on`, `try` (only if OS supports read-ahead advice). Limited by wal_decode_buffer_size and maintenance_io_concurrency.
How far ahead in WAL the server can look to find blocks to prefetch.

Shell command to fetch an archived WAL segment. `%f` file name, `%p` destination path (relative to data dir), `%r` file containing the last valid restart point, `%%`. Required for archive recovery, optional for streaming. Must return nonzero for files not in the archive. Killed by signal (other than SIGTERM) or shell error => recovery aborts, server will not start. Example `restore_command = 'cp /mnt/server/archivedir/%f "%p"'`.

Shell command run at every restartpoint to remove no-longer-needed archived WAL; `%r`. Example `archive_cleanup_command = 'pg_archivecleanup /mnt/server/archivedir %r'`. Nonzero exit => warning; signal/shell error => fatal.
Shell command run once at end of recovery; `%r`. Nonzero => warning, startup proceeds; signal/shell error => no startup.
Only allowed value `'immediate'`: end recovery as soon as a consistent state is reached (end of the online backup).
Timestamp (timestamptz format; no tz abbreviations unless timezone_abbreviations set earlier; prefer numeric UTC offset or full zone name).
Transaction ID; transactions that committed before (and optionally including) it are recovered. XIDs are assigned at start but complete in a different order.
Stop just after (on) or just before (off) the target; applies to lsn/time/xid.
Numeric timeline ID (hex with `0x`; WAL file `00000011000000A10000004F` => timeline 0x11 = 17), `current` (timeline current when base backup was taken), or `latest` (latest timeline in archive).

`pause` (resume with `pg_wal_replay_resume()`), `promote`, `shutdown` (recovery.signal is not removed, so subsequent starts shut down immediately until config changed or file removed). No effect without a target. If hot_standby is off, pause acts like shutdown. If archive recovery ends before the target is reached, server shuts down with a fatal error.
Enables the WAL summarizer process (primary or standby). Cannot start with wal_level=minimal.
Age after which WAL summaries are auto-removed (by file timestamp); 0 = never.
Max concurrent WAL sender processes (standbys + streaming base backup clients). 0 disables replication. Needs wal_level >= replica. Standby must be >= primary.
Max replication slots. Lower than existing slot count prevents startup. Needs wal_level >= replica.

Libraries in dynamic_library_path trusted as logical output plugins; requests for other libraries are refused (`ERROR: library "..." may not be used as an output plugin`). Applies to all users. Plugin name must match a list entry exactly. The defaults: `pgoutput` = core plugin for logical replication (removing it breaks subscription connections and slot maintenance); `test_decoding` = human-readable text decoding, default for `pg_recvlogical`. Helper: `SELECT DISTINCT plugin FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE plugin IS NOT NULL;`
Minimum size of past WAL kept in `pg_wal` for standbys. If a standby falls behind by more, the needed segment may be removed and the replication connection terminated (recoverable from archive).

Max WAL that replication slots may retain in pg_wal at checkpoint time; if a slot's `restart_lsn` falls behind current LSN by more, the slot's standby may be unable to continue. See `pg_replication_slots`.

Invalidate slots inactive longer than this; invalidation happens at checkpoint; uses `pg_replication_slots.inactive_since`. Not applicable to slots that do not reserve WAL or synced standby slots (`synced` = true).
Terminate replication connections inactive longer than this (detect standby crash/network outage). 0 disables.

List of standbys that can be synchronous. Syntaxes: `[FIRST] num_sync ( standby_name [, ...] )` (priority-based; earlier names have higher priority; others are potential sync standbys; a disconnected sync standby is replaced immediately by the next-highest priority), `ANY num_sync ( standby_name [, ...] )` (quorum-based: commit proceeds once any num_sync reply), `standby_name [, ...]` (pre-9.6; = `FIRST 1 (...)`). `*` matches any name. Standby name = standby's `application_name` (physical: from primary_conninfo, default cluster_name else `walreceiver`; logical: subscription name). Compared case-insensitively. Only standbys in state `streaming` in `pg_stat_replication` count.

Comma-separated physical standby slot names that logical WAL senders wait for before sending decoded changes to plugins (so logical failover slots never get ahead of the physical standbys). Logical replication stalls if listed slots do not exist/are invalidated. `pg_replication_slot_advance`, `pg_logical_slot_get_changes`, `pg_logical_slot_peek_changes` on failover slots also block. Those standbys must set `sync_replication_slots = true`.

Connection string to the sending server (libpq format). Password may come from `~/.pgpass` (database name `replication`). A `dbname` is needed for replication slot synchronization only. Changing it restarts the WAL receiver.
Existing replication slot to use on the sender. Change restarts WAL receiver.
Allow connections and queries during recovery.

How long standby waits before cancelling queries conflicting with WAL to apply, when WAL is read from archive. -1 = wait forever. It is the max total time to apply any one WAL segment's data, not a per-query grace.
Same for WAL received via streaming: max total time to apply WAL once received. -1 = forever.
WAL receiver creates a temporary slot on the remote when no primary_slot_name.
Max time between WAL receiver progress reports (written, flushed, applied positions) to the upstream (`pg_stat_replication`).

Standby sends feedback about its running queries to the primary; eliminates query cancels due to cleanup records but can cause bloat on the primary. Not more often than once per wal_receiver_status_interval; passed upstream in cascades. Timestamp-based (clock jumps can break it).
Terminate inactive replication connections (detect primary crash/outage). 0 disables.
Wait before retrying when WAL is unavailable from any source (streaming, pg_wal, archive). Also limits respawn rate of failing logical apply/tablesync workers.

Delayed standby: replay each commit only when standby system time >= primary commit time + delay. Delay applies only to commit records (other records replayed ASAP; MVCC hides them until the commit record is applied). Starts once consistent state reached; ends on promotion. With `synchronous_commit=remote_apply` every COMMIT waits. Delays hot_standby_feedback.
Physical standby synchronizes logical failover slots from the primary so subscribers can resume after failover.

How many replication origins can be tracked simultaneously (limits subscriptions; at least number of subscriptions plus reserve for table sync). Lower than current tracked (`pg_replication_origin_status`) prevents startup.
Max logical replication workers (leader apply, parallel apply, table sync); taken from max_worker_processes.
Max table synchronization workers per subscription (initial copy parallelism); one sync worker per table; from max_logical_replication_workers pool.
Max parallel apply workers per subscription (for `streaming = parallel`).
Reordering DISTINCT keys to match the input path's pathkeys
GROUP BY keys sorted in the order of a child node's keys (e.g. index scan); off => only sorted to match ORDER BY
Index-only scans (enable_indexscan must also be on)
Materialization; cannot be suppressed entirely (off = only where required for correctness)
Memoize: cache results of parameterized scans inside nested-loop joins; less-used entries evicted when space needed
Nested-loop joins; cannot be suppressed entirely, off only discourages
Hash joins with parallel hash (no effect unless hash joins enabled)
Plan-time partition elimination AND plans that let the executor prune partitions at run time

Join partitioned tables by joining matching partitions; requires join conditions including all partition keys, same data type, one-to-one matching child partitions. Multiplies work_mem-limited nodes by partition count; planning much costlier.
Per-partition grouping/aggregation; if GROUP BY lacks the partition keys only partial aggregation per partition, finalize later. Same memory/planning caveats.
Provide input presorted for ORDER BY / DISTINCT aggregates instead of always sorting in the executor
Replace self joins with semantically equivalent single scans (plain tables only)
Sequential scans; cannot be suppressed entirely, off only discourages
Explicit sort steps; cannot be suppressed entirely
Disk page fetch that is part of a series of sequential fetches. Per-tablespace override (ALTER TABLESPACE).

Non-sequentially-fetched disk page. Per-tablespace override. Lower => prefers index scans. Real random access is much more than 4x sequential, but 4.0 assumes most random accesses (indexed reads) hit cache. Setting below seq_page_cost is "not physically sensible"; equal makes sense for a fully RAM-cached database; heavily cached => lower both relative to CPU costs.
Processing each index entry during an index scan.
Processing each operator or function executed.
Transferring one tuple from a parallel worker to another process.
Min table data to be scanned for a parallel scan to be considered.
Min index data (pages the planner believes will be touched) for a parallel index scan; also decides whether an index can participate in parallel VACUUM.
Planner's assumption of disk cache available to a single query (shared buffers + kernel cache for PG files). Higher => index scans more likely. Estimation only: allocates nothing, reserves nothing.
Query cost above which JIT compilation is activated; -1 disables JIT.
Cost above which JIT inlines functions/operators; -1 disables inlining; not meaningful below jit_above_cost.
Cost above which JIT applies expensive optimizations; -1 disables.
Use GEQO for queries with at least this many FROM items (a FULL OUTER JOIN construct counts as one).
Range 1-10; only used to compute defaults of the other GEQO variables.
0 (auto from geqo_effort and number of tables)
Individuals in the genetic population; at least 2, useful 100-1000.
Initial random seed, range 0-1; changes the set of join paths explored.
Default statistics target for columns without `ALTER TABLE SET STATISTICS`. Larger => slower ANALYZE, better estimates.

`on` (all tables), `off`, `partition` (only inheritance child tables and UNION ALL subqueries). Planner compares query conditions with CHECK constraints and skips contradicted tables. Example: `CREATE TABLE child1000(check (key between 1000 and 1999)) INHERITS(parent); ... SELECT * FROM parent WHERE key = 2400;` skips child1000. Declarative partitioning uses `enable_partition_pruning` instead.
Estimated fraction of a cursor's rows that will be fetched; small => "fast start" plans; 1.0 => planned like regular queries.
Merge sub-queries into upper query if resulting FROM list has no more than this many items. Setting >= geqo_threshold may trigger GEQO.
Whether JIT compilation may be used, if available.
Rewrite explicit JOINs (except FULL JOINs) into FROM lists of no more than this many items. **1 = no reordering: explicit join order is the actual join order.**
`auto`, `force_custom_plan`, `force_generic_plan`. Custom plan = replanned per execution with parameter values; generic plan = reused. Considered when a cached plan is executed, not when prepared.
Estimated average size of a recursive query's working table as a multiple of the non-recursive term's estimated size. 1.0 for low fan-out (shortest path); larger for graph analytics.

Comma-separated: `stderr`, `csvlog`, `jsonlog`, `syslog`, (Windows) `eventlog`. csvlog/jsonlog need logging_collector. File `current_logfiles` records the files in use (e.g. `stderr log/postgresql.log`).
Background process capturing stderr into log files. Designed never to drop messages (backends may block under extreme load; syslog instead drops). No durability guarantee.
Directory for log files (absolute or relative to data dir).
File name pattern; `.csv` / `.json` replace a trailing `.log` for those formats.
Log file permissions (0640 for group read).
Max lifetime of a log file; 0 disables time-based rotation.
Max log file size; 0 disables size-based rotation.
Truncate rather than append on time-based rotation only (not startup or size-based). Example 7-day ring: log_filename `server_log.%a`, truncate on, age 1440.
Prefix each message with increasing sequence number (defeats "last message repeated N times").
Split messages by lines and to fit 1024 bytes.
Levels in order: DEBUG5, DEBUG4, DEBUG3, DEBUG2, DEBUG1, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR, LOG, FATAL, PANIC (each includes all that follow). **LOG ranks differently here than in client_min_messages.**
Log the SQL statement for messages of this severity or higher; PANIC effectively disables.
Log duration (and text) of statements running at least this long; 0 logs all. Overrides log_min_duration_sample. With extended protocol, Parse/Bind/Execute durations logged independently.
Statements at least this long are candidates for sampled logging.
Fraction of statements exceeding log_min_duration_sample that are logged.
Fraction of transactions whose statements are ALL logged, regardless of duration.
Startup process logs a message about a long-running operation after this time and at this interval; 0 disables.
Any string of less than NAMEDATALEN chars (64 in a standard build => max 63); shown in `pg_stat_activity`, CSV logs, `%a`. Printable ASCII only.
Print the parse tree of each query at LOG level.
Indent the output of the `debug_print_*` parameters.
Log autovacuum actions running at least this long; 0 = all; -1 = disabled. Any value other than -1 also logs skips due to conflicting lock or concurrently dropped relation.
Log checkpoints and restartpoints with statistics (buffers written, write time).

Comma-separated list of aspects: `receipt`, `authentication`, `authorization`, `setup_durations` (total setup, fork time, authentication time), `all`. Legacy booleans still accepted; positive = receipt, authentication, authorization. Failed authentication is always logged.
Log session termination with session duration.
Log duration of every completed statement (without query text, unlike log_min_duration_statement=0).
`TERSE` (no DETAIL, HINT, QUERY, CONTEXT), `DEFAULT`, `VERBOSE` (adds SQLSTATE, source file, function, line).
Also log host name of connecting host (DNS cost).
Log when a session waits longer than `deadlock_timeout` for a lock.
Detailed log when a lock acquisition fails; currently only failures due to `SELECT NOWAIT`. (New in 18.)
Log when the startup process waits longer than deadlock_timeout for recovery conflicts.
Trim bind parameter values logged with non-error statement logs; 0 disables logging them.
Trim bind parameter values in error messages; -1 = full. Adds overhead (text copies stored at statement start).

`none`, `ddl` (CREATE/ALTER/DROP), `mod` (ddl + INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, COPY FROM), `all`. Statements with simple syntax errors are not logged even with `all`. May reveal plaintext passwords.
Log each replication command and walsender slot acquisition/release.
Log each temp file (sorts, hashes, temp query results) name and size (bytes) when deleted, if size >= this; 0 = all. **The way to observe work_mem spills.**
GMT built-in (initdb writes the system zone)
Time zone for log timestamps; cluster-wide.
Name shown in the process title of all server processes; default application_name for a standby connection. Less than NAMEDATALEN (64) chars, printable ASCII.
Update process title each time a new SQL command is received.
Collect each session's currently executing command, its identifier and start time. Visible only to superusers, roles with `pg_read_all_stats`, and the session owner.
Memory reserved per session for `pg_stat_activity.query` text.
Collect statistics on database activity; **required by autovacuum**.
Time cost-based vacuum delay; shown in `pg_stat_progress_vacuum`, `pg_stat_progress_analyze`, VACUUM/ANALYZE VERBOSE, autovacuum logs. (New in 18.)

Time database I/O waits; shown in `pg_stat_database`, `pg_stat_io` (object not wal), `pg_stat_get_backend_io()`, `EXPLAIN (BUFFERS)`, VACUUM VERBOSE, autovacuum logs, pg_stat_statements. Overhead from clock reads: measure with `pg_test_timing`.
Time WAL I/O waits; shown in `pg_stat_io` for object `wal` and `pg_stat_get_backend_io()`.
`none`, `pl` (procedural-language functions only), `all` (also SQL and C). Inlined SQL functions are never tracked.

Behaviour for repeated stats access within a transaction: `none` (re-fetch from shared memory each time; best for monitoring), `cache` (first access to an object's stats caches it until end of transaction), `snapshot` (first access caches all stats of current database). `pg_stat_clear_snapshot()` discards; changing the setting in a transaction discards the snapshot.

In-core query identifier computation: `off`, `on`, `auto` (modules such as pg_stat_statements enable it), `regress` (like auto but not shown in EXPLAIN). Query id appears in `pg_stat_activity`, EXPLAIN, `%Q`.
Log total per-statement performance statistics (getrusage-like). Cannot be enabled together with the per-module options.
Run the autovacuum launcher daemon. Needs `track_counts`. **Even when off, autovacuum processes are launched if necessary to prevent transaction ID wraparound.**
Backend slots reserved for autovacuum workers. (New in 18.)
Max autovacuum workers (excluding launcher) running at once; values above autovacuum_worker_slots have no effect.
Minimum delay between autovacuum runs on any given database.
Minimum updated or deleted tuples to trigger VACUUM.
Inserted tuples to trigger VACUUM; -1 disables insert-triggered vacuum.
Minimum inserted, updated or deleted tuples to trigger ANALYZE.
Upper limit on the value computed from vacuum_threshold + scale_factor; -1 = no cap. (New in 18.)
postmaster (can only be reduced per table)
Max age of `pg_class.relfrozenxid` before a VACUUM is forced to prevent XID wraparound. Relatively low because vacuum also allows removal of old `pg_xact` files.
Max age of `pg_class.relminmxid` before forced VACUUM; allows removal of old `pg_multixact/members` and `pg_multixact/offsets` files.
Cost delay for automatic VACUUM; -1 = use vacuum_cost_delay.
Cost limit for automatic VACUUM; **distributed proportionally among running autovacuum workers** so the sum does not exceed it.
Sleep time when cost limit exceeded. Useful values are small, perhaps < 1 ms.
Vacuuming a buffer found in shared buffer cache (lock buffer pool, look up shared hash table, scan the page).
Buffer that has to be read from disk.
Charged when vacuum modifies a block that was previously clean (extra I/O to flush it again).
Accumulated cost that causes the sleep.

VACUUM/autovacuum try to truncate empty pages at the end of the table and return space to the OS; **requires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock**. Overridden by VACUUM's `TRUNCATE` option and per-table storage parameter. (GUC new in 18.)

VACUUM performs an **aggressive scan** when `pg_class.relfrozenxid` reaches this age: visits every page that might contain unfrozen XIDs or MXIDs, not just those that might contain dead tuples. Range: 0 to 2 billion. Clamp: silently limited to 95% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age.
Cutoff age VACUUM uses to decide whether to trigger freezing of pages that have an older XID. Range: 0 to 1 billion. Clamp: limited to half of autovacuum_freeze_max_age.

Last-resort failsafe: cost-based delay no longer applied, non-essential tasks (index vacuuming) bypassed, Buffer Access Strategy disabled (VACUUM may use all of shared buffers). Range: 0 to 2.1 billion. Clamp: no less than 105% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age.
Aggressive scan when `pg_class.relminmxid` reaches this age. Range: 0 to 2 billion. Clamp: 95% of autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age.
Cutoff age for freezing pages with an older multixact ID. Range: 0 to 1 billion. Clamp: half of autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age.
Multixact failsafe (delay dropped, index vacuuming bypassed). Range: 0 to 2.1 billion. Clamp: no less than 105% of autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age.

Max fraction of the relation's pages that VACUUM may scan and fail to set all-frozen in the visibility map before disabling **eager scanning**; 0 disables eager scanning. Only failures count; successful eager freezes are capped internally at 20% of the all-visible-but-not-all-frozen pages. Per-table storage parameter override. (New in 18.) Range: -. Clamp: -.
Levels sent to client: DEBUG5, DEBUG4, DEBUG3, DEBUG2, DEBUG1, LOG, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR. INFO is always sent. LOG ranks differently than in log_min_messages.
Schema search order for unqualified names (see rules below).
Off => queries that would apply at least one row security policy raise an error instead (pg_dump sets off). No effect for superusers and BYPASSRLS roles.
Table AM for CREATE TABLE / materialized view without explicit AM and for SELECT ... INTO.

Default tablespace for tables and indexes. Not used for temp tables (temp_tablespaces) nor CREATE DATABASE. A non-empty value at partitioned-table creation becomes that table's tablespace for future partitions.
Default TOAST compression for compressible columns: `pglz`, `lz4` (if built --with-lz4). Per-column `COMPRESSION` option overrides.
Tablespaces for temporary objects and temp files for sorting; random member per object, successive members within a transaction.
Off disables validation of routine body during CREATE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE (pg_dump sets off).
Read-only transactions cannot alter non-temporary tables.
For serializable read-only transactions: may be delayed before proceeding, then runs without serializability overhead or abort risk. No effect on read-write or lower isolation levels.
Reflects current transaction's isolation level; setting it = SET TRANSACTION.

`origin`, `replica`, `local`. `replica` => triggers and rules in default configuration do not fire; **also disables all foreign key checks** (FKs are triggers). origin and local treated the same internally. Changing it discards cached plans.

Abort any statement taking longer. Measured from command arrival until completion; applied per statement in a multi-statement simple-query message (before 13: whole string). Extended protocol: starts at Parse/Bind/Execute/Describe, cancelled by completion of Execute or Sync. Not recommended in postgresql.conf.

Terminate any session spending longer than this in a transaction (explicit or implicit single-statement). If <= idle_in_transaction_session_timeout or statement_timeout the longer timeout is ignored. Prepared transactions are not subject.
Abort any statement that waits longer than this to acquire a lock (table, index, row, other object); applies separately to each lock acquisition attempt, explicit or implicit.
Terminate sessions idle within an open transaction longer than this (they hold locks and prevent vacuuming recently-dead tuples => bloat).
Terminate sessions idle outside a transaction longer than this. Be wary with connection poolers.
`base64` or `hex` for binary values in XML.
`DOCUMENT` or `CONTENT`; also `SET XML OPTION { DOCUMENT | CONTENT };`.
Max size of a GIN index's pending list (fastupdate); when exceeded the list is flushed in bulk into the main GIN structure. Per-index storage parameter override.
For CREATEROLE non-superusers: newly created role is granted back to the creator with options `set`, `inherit`, or both.
False disables all event triggers (for repairing faulty ones).
Comma-separated relation kinds for which access to non-system relations is prohibited: `view`, `foreign-table`.
`ISO, MDY` built-in (initdb writes a value matching lc_time)
Two components: output format (`ISO`, `Postgres`, `SQL`, `German`) and field order (`DMY`, `MDY`, `YMD`); `Euro`/`European` = DMY; `US`/`NonEuro`/`NonEuropean` = MDY.
Time zone for displaying and interpreting timestamps.

>= 1 (up to 3): shortest-precise output (at most 17 digits for float8, 9 for float4; round-trips exactly). <= 0: rounded to FLT_DIG/DBL_DIG reduced by the value (-1 => float4 5 digits, float8 14 digits). Meaning and default changed in PostgreSQL 12.
Locale for formatting dates and times.
Message level for ICU locale validation problems: DISABLED, DEBUG5..DEBUG1, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR, LOG.
Text search configuration used when none is given explicitly.
user (takes effect only at connection start)

Libraries preloaded at connection start; restricted to the `plugins` subdirectory of the library directory (`$libdir/plugins/mylib` or just `mylib`). Missing library => connection fails. Typically set via PGOPTIONS or ALTER ROLE SET.
Libraries preloaded at connection start (e.g. `auto_explain` for one role via ALTER ROLE SET); no restart needed.

Libraries preloaded at server start; required for libraries that allocate shared memory, reserve light-weight locks, or start background workers (e.g. pg_stat_statements). Missing library => server fails to start. On Windows each process re-loads them.
JIT provider library; non-existent => JIT unavailable but no error.
Colon-separated (semicolon on Windows) absolute directories searched for modules named without a slash in CREATE FUNCTION/LOAD. `$libdir` = `pg_config --pkglibdir`. Empty disables search.

Path searched for extension control files (`name.control`); each element is expected to have an `extension` subdirectory (suffix appended automatically); `$system` = `pg_config --sharedir`; first match wins. Usually set together with dynamic_library_path. (New in 18.)
Soft upper limit on the size of the set returned by GIN index scans.

Time to wait on a lock before running the (relatively expensive) deadlock check; optimistic assumption that deadlocks are rare. 1s is "probably about the smallest value you would want in practice"; ideally exceed typical transaction time. Also the threshold for `log_lock_waits` and `log_recovery_conflict_waits` messages.

Shared lock table has space for this many objects (e.g. tables) **per server process or prepared transaction**; it limits the *average*, a single transaction may lock more if everything fits. Not a row limit (row locks are unlimited). Raise for queries touching many tables (e.g. parent with many partitions). Standby must be >= primary.
Same sizing rule for the shared predicate (SIREAD) lock table used by SERIALIZABLE.
Pages/tuples of one relation that can be predicate-locked before promotion to a whole-relation lock. >= 0 absolute; negative = max_pred_locks_per_transaction / abs(value) (default -2 => 32).
Rows on one page that can be predicate-locked before promotion to a page lock.
Array input parser treats unquoted `NULL` as a null element (pre-8.2 treated it as the string "NULL").

Whether `\'` may represent a quote in non-standard-conforming literals (incl. `E'...'`): `on`, `off`, `safe_encoding` (allow only if client encoding cannot contain ASCII `\` inside a multibyte char). SQL-injection risk motivation.
Warn when backslash appears in an ordinary `'...'` literal and standard_conforming_strings is off.
Disable large-object privilege checks introduced in 9.0.
Force quoting of all identifiers in generated SQL (EXPLAIN, pg_get_viewdef).
Ordinary literals treat backslashes literally; use `E'...'` for escapes.

Concurrent seqscans of large tables synchronize (a scan may start mid-table and wrap around) => **row order without ORDER BY can change unpredictably**. off = pre-8.3 behaviour (always start at block 0).
Treat `expr = NULL` as `expr IS NULL` (MS Access compatibility). Only the literal `= NULL` form; not IN etc.

Off => ALTER SYSTEM raises an error. **Not a security feature** (superusers can still write postgresql.auto.conf via shell); for externally managed configuration. postgresql.auto.conf still takes effect.
Any error terminates the session (normally only FATAL does).
Automatically reinitialize after a backend crash; turn off when clusterware should take control.

Off => **PANIC on failure to flush modified data files** (server crashes, recovers from WAL), because after a write-back failure the kernel page cache state is unknown and a retry may falsely succeed. on => report error and retry at a later checkpoint (only after studying the OS's behaviour).

Before crash recovery: `fsync` recursively opens and fsyncs every file in the data directory (following symlinks for pg_wal and tablespaces only); `syncfs` (Linux) syncs whole file systems (faster, but affected by other apps' dirty data; before Linux 5.8 I/O errors may not be reported). Applies to any start after an unclean shutdown, including pg_basebackup copies.
Disk block size; affects meaning of block-unit GUCs such as shared_buffers.
Permissions the data directory had at startup (always 0700 on Windows); see `initdb -g`.
Actual huge-page state (unknown with `postgres -C`); check result of `huge_pages=try`.
Server currently in hot standby (all transactions read-only); changes in-session only on promotion.
NAMEDATALEN - 1 (NAMEDATALEN 64); bytes, so fewer characters in multibyte encodings.
Semaphores needed, based on max_connections, **autovacuum_max_workers** (wording of this page; 18.4.1 says autovacuum_worker_slots), max_wal_senders, max_worker_processes, etc.
Blocks per relation file segment (RELSEG_SIZE); segment bytes = segment_size * block_size = 1GB default.
Database encoding, fixed at CREATE DATABASE.
Main shared memory area size, rounded up to nearest MB.
Huge pages needed for main shared memory based on huge_page_size; Linux only.
SSL library the server was built with.

Allow structural modification of system tables (otherwise forbidden even to superusers).
Comma-separated C function names; an error raised in one of them writes a backtrace to the log.
Pass all parse/plan trees through copyObject() (needs DEBUG_NODE_TESTS_ENABLED, auto with --enable-cassert).

1 = invalidate every catalog cache entry at first opportunity (catalog caching effectively off; very slow); higher = recursive. Needs DISCARD_CACHES_ENABLED (cassert builds); always 0 in production builds.
Direct I/O (O_DIRECT / F_NOCACHE / FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING) for `data`, `wal`, `wal_init`; currently reduces performance.

`on` adds a Gather on top of every parallel-safe plan so it runs in a worker; `regress` also hides the Gather in EXPLAIN and the worker context line. Use to find functions that should be PARALLEL UNSAFE/RESTRICTED.
Walk raw DML parse trees with raw_expression_tree_walker() (cassert builds).
Ignore system indexes when reading system tables (still updated); for damaged system indexes.
Seconds to delay after authentication (attach debugger).
Seconds to delay right after fork, before authentication.
Debug output for LISTEN/NOTIFY (needs DEBUG1 message level).
Emit resource usage during sort operations.

Dump heavyweight lock operations (lock id tuple, grantMask, req/grant counts per mode, wait mask, lock type). LOCK_DEBUG builds; structure in `src/include/storage/lock.h`. Lightweight lock usage (LOCK_DEBUG). LWLocks protect shared-memory data structures.
Same as trace_locks for advisory locks (LOCK_DEBUG).
Do not trace locks on tables below this OID (LOCK_DEBUG).
Unconditionally trace locks on this table OID (LOCK_DEBUG).
Dump all current locks when a deadlock timeout occurs (LOCK_DEBUG).
Resource usage for B-tree operations (BTREE_BUILD_STATS builds).

Add FPIs to WAL records and, on replay, compare buffers with the images (FATAL on unexpected difference; hint-bit variations ignored). `all` or list of resource managers: heap, heap2, btree, hash, gin, gist, sequence, spgist, brin, generic.
With data checksums: warn instead of error on checksum failure and continue (may crash, propagate/hide corruption). Corrupt header still errors.

Damaged page header => warning, page zeroed **in memory**, processing continues; destroys all rows on that page; zeroed pages are not forced to disk, so recreate the table/index before turning off.
During recovery, ignore WAL references to invalid pages (warn) instead of PANIC.
Write generated LLVM IR into data_directory.
JIT-compile expressions when JIT is active.
JIT-compile tuple deforming when JIT is active.
Remove temporary files after a backend crash.
After a backend crash, send children SIGABRT (core dumps) instead of SIGQUIT.
Send SIGABRT instead of SIGKILL to children still alive 5 seconds after SIGQUIT.

`immediate`: publisher streams/serializes each change instead of waiting for logical_decoding_work_mem; subscriber leader (streaming=parallel) serializes all changes to files instead of the shared memory queue.

title: Glossary
rows: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. This set of properties of database transactions is intended to guarantee validity in concurrent operation and even in event of errors, power failures, etc.
A function that combines (aggregates) multiple input values, for example by counting, averaging or adding, yielding a single output value. See also: Window function (routine).
Interfaces which PostgreSQL use in order to access data in tables and indexes. This abstraction allows for adding support for new types of data storage.

The act of collecting statistics from data in tables and other relations to help the query planner to make decisions about how to execute queries. (Don't confuse this term with the ANALYZE option to the EXPLAIN command.)

Asynchronous I/O (AIO) describes performing I/O in a non-blocking way (asynchronously), in contrast to synchronous I/O, which blocks for the entire duration of the I/O. With AIO, starting an I/O operation is separated from waiting for the result of the operation, allowing multiple I/O operations to be initiated concurrently, as well as performing CPU heavy operations concurrently with I/O. The price for that increased concurrency is increased complexity. See also: Input/Output.
In reference to a datum: the fact that its value cannot be broken down into smaller components. In reference to a database transaction: see atomicity.

The property of a transaction that either all its operations complete as a single unit or none do. In addition, if a system failure occurs during the execution of a transaction, no partial results are visible after recovery. This is one of the ACID properties.
An element with a certain name and data type found within a tuple.

A set of background processes that routinely perform vacuum and analyze operations. The auxiliary process that coordinates the work and is always present (unless autovacuum is disabled) is known as the autovacuum launcher, and the processes that carry out the tasks are known as the autovacuum workers.

A process within an instance that is in charge of some specific background task for the instance. The auxiliary processes consist of the autovacuum launcher (but not the autovacuum workers), the background writer, the checkpointer, the logger, the startup process, the WAL archiver, the WAL receiver (but not the WAL senders), the WAL summarizer, and the WAL writer.
Process of an instance which acts on behalf of a client session and handles its requests. (Don't confuse this term with the similar terms Background Worker or Background Writer).

Process within an instance, which runs system- or user-supplied code. Serves as infrastructure for several features in PostgreSQL, such as logical replication and parallel queries. In addition, Extensions can add custom background worker processes.

An auxiliary process that writes dirty data pages from shared memory to the file system. It wakes up periodically, but works only for a short period in order to distribute its expensive I/O activity over time to avoid generating larger I/O peaks which could block other processes.

A binary copy of all database cluster files. It is generated by the tool pg_basebackup. In combination with WAL files it can be used as the starting point for recovery, log shipping, or streaming replication.
Space in data pages which does not contain current row versions, such as unused (free) space or outdated row versions.

The first user initialized in a database cluster. This user owns all system catalog tables in each database. It is also the role from which all granted permissions originate. Because of these things, this role may not be dropped. This role also behaves as a normal database superuser, and its superuser status cannot be removed.

Some operations will access a large number of pages. A Buffer Access Strategy helps to prevent these operations from evicting too many pages from shared buffers. A Buffer Access Strategy sets up references to a limited number of shared buffers and reuses them circularly. When the operation requires a new page, a victim buffer is chosen from the buffers in the strategy ring, which may require flushing the page's dirty data and possibly also unflushed WAL to permanent storage. Buffer Access Strategies are used for various operations such as sequential scans of large tables, VACUUM, COPY, CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, ALTER TABLE, CREATE DATABASE, CREATE INDEX, and CLUSTER.
A conversion of a datum from its current data type to another data type.
The SQL standard uses this term to indicate what is called a database in PostgreSQL's terminology. (Don't confuse this term with system catalog).

A type of constraint defined on a relation which restricts the values allowed in one or more attributes. The check constraint can make reference to any attribute of the same row in the relation, but cannot reference other rows of the same relation or other relations.

A point in the WAL sequence at which it is guaranteed that the heap and index data files have been updated with all information from shared memory modified before that checkpoint; a checkpoint record is written and flushed to WAL to mark that point. A checkpoint is also the act of carrying out all the actions that are necessary to reach a checkpoint as defined above. This process is initiated when predefined conditions are met, such as a specified amount of time has passed, or a certain volume of records has been written; or it can be invoked by the user with the command CHECKPOINT.
An auxiliary process that is responsible for executing checkpoints.
Any process, possibly remote, that establishes a session by connecting to an instance to interact with a database.

The operating system user that owns the data directory and under which the postgres process is run. It is required that this user exist prior to creating a new database cluster. On operating systems with a root user, said user is not allowed to be the cluster owner.
An attribute found in a table or view.
The act of finalizing a transaction within the database, which makes it visible to other transactions and assures its durability.
The concept that multiple independent operations happen within the database at the same time. In PostgreSQL, concurrency is controlled by the multiversion concurrency control mechanism.
An established line of communication between a client process and a backend process, usually over a network, supporting a session. This term is sometimes used as a synonym for session.

The property that the data in the database is always in compliance with integrity constraints. Transactions may be allowed to violate some of the constraints transiently before it commits, but if such violations are not resolved by the time it commits, such a transaction is automatically rolled back. This is one of the ACID properties.
A restriction on the values of data allowed within a table, or in attributes of a domain.
A system which, if enabled, accumulates statistical information about the instance's activities.
A named collection of local SQL objects.

A collection of databases and global SQL objects, and their common static and dynamic metadata. Sometimes referred to as a cluster. A database cluster is created using the initdb program. In PostgreSQL, the term cluster is also sometimes used to refer to an instance. (Don't confuse this term with the SQL command CLUSTER.) See also cluster owner, the operating-system owner of a cluster, and bootstrap superuser, the PostgreSQL owner of a cluster.
A role having superuser status. Frequently referred to as superuser.

The base directory on the file system of a server that contains all data files and subdirectories associated with a database cluster (with the exception of tablespaces, and optionally WAL). The environment variable PGDATA is commonly used to refer to the data directory. A cluster's storage space comprises the data directory plus any additional tablespaces.

The basic structure used to store relation data. All pages are of the same size. Data pages are typically stored on disk, each in a specific file, and can be read to shared buffers where they can be modified, becoming dirty. They become clean when written to disk. New pages, which initially exist in memory only, are also dirty until written.
The internal representation of one value of an SQL data type.
An SQL command which removes rows from a given table or relation.
A user-defined data type that is based on another underlying data type. It acts the same as the underlying type except for possibly restricting the set of allowed values.
The assurance that once a transaction has been committed, the changes remain even after a system failure or crash. This is one of the ACID properties.
A software add-on package that can be installed on an instance to get extra features.

A physical file which stores data for a given relation. File segments are limited in size by a configuration value (typically 1 gigabyte), so if a relation exceeds that size, it is split into multiple segments. (Don't confuse this term with the similar term WAL segment).

A means of representing data that is not contained in the local database so that it appears as if were in local table(s). With a foreign data wrapper it is possible to define a foreign server and foreign tables.
A type of constraint defined on one or more columns in a table which requires the value(s) in those columns to identify zero or one row in another (or, infrequently, the same) table.
A named collection of foreign tables which all use the same foreign data wrapper and have other configuration values in common.

A relation which appears to have rows and columns similar to a regular table, but will forward requests for data through its foreign data wrapper, which will return result sets structured according to the definition of the foreign table.

Each of the separate segmented file sets in which a relation is stored. The main fork is where the actual data resides. There also exist two secondary forks for metadata: the free space map and the visibility map. Unlogged relations also have an init fork.

A storage structure that keeps metadata about each data page of a table's main fork. The free space map entry for each page stores the amount of free space that's available for future tuples, and is structured to be efficiently searched for available space for a new tuple of a given size.

A type of routine that receives zero or more arguments, returns zero or more output values, and is constrained to run within one transaction. Functions are invoked as part of a query, for example via SELECT. Certain functions can return sets; those are called set-returning functions. Functions can also be used for triggers to invoke.
An SQL command that is used to allow a user or role to access specific objects within the database.
Contains the values of row attributes (i.e., the data) for a relation. The heap is realized within one or more file segments in the relation's main fork.
A computer that communicates with other computers over a network. This is sometimes used as a synonym for server. It is also used to refer to a computer where client processes run.
A relation that contains data derived from a table or materialized view. Its internal structure supports fast retrieval of and access to the original data.

A special base backup that for some files may contain only those pages that were modified since a previous backup, as opposed to the full contents of every file. Like base backups, it is generated by the tool pg_basebackup. To restore incremental backups the tool pg_combinebackup is used, which combines incremental backups with a base backup. Afterwards, recovery can use WAL to bring the database cluster to a consistent state.

Input/Output (I/O) describes the communication between a program and peripheral devices. In the context of database systems, I/O commonly, but not exclusively, refers to interaction with storage devices or the network. See also: Asynchronous I/O.
An SQL command used to add new data into a table.

A group of backend and auxiliary processes that communicate using a common shared memory area. One postmaster process manages the instance; one instance manages exactly one database cluster with all its databases. Many instances can run on the same server as long as their TCP ports do not conflict. The instance handles all key features of a DBMS: read and write access to files and shared memory, assurance of the ACID properties, connections to client processes, privilege verification, crash recovery, replication, etc.
The property that the effects of a transaction are not visible to concurrent transactions before it commits. This is one of the ACID properties.
An operation and SQL keyword used in queries for combining data from multiple relations.
A means of identifying a row within a table or other relation by values contained within one or more attributes in that relation.
A mechanism that allows a process to limit or prevent simultaneous access to a resource.
Log files contain human-readable text lines about events. Examples include login failures, long-running queries, etc.

A table is considered logged if changes to it are sent to the WAL. By default, all regular tables are logged. A table can be specified as unlogged either at creation time or via the ALTER TABLE command.

An auxiliary process which, if enabled, writes information about database events into the current log file. When reaching certain time- or volume-dependent criteria, a new log file is created. Also called syslogger.
A set of publisher and subscriber instances with the publisher instance replicating changes to the subscriber instance.
Archaic term for a WAL record.
Byte offset into the WAL, increasing monotonically with each new WAL record.

The property that some information has been pre-computed and stored for later use, rather than computing it on-the-fly. This term is used in materialized view, to mean that the data derived from the view's query is stored on disk separately from the sources of that data. This term is also used to refer to some multi-step queries to mean that the data resulting from executing a given step is stored in memory (with the possibility of spilling to disk), so that it can be read multiple times by another step.
A relation that is defined by a SELECT statement (just like a view), but stores data in the same way that a table does. It cannot be modified via INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE operations.
An SQL command used to conditionally add, modify, or remove rows in a given table, using data from a source relation.

A mechanism designed to allow several transactions to be reading and writing the same rows without one process causing other processes to stall. In PostgreSQL, MVCC is implemented by creating copies (versions) of tuples as they are modified; after transactions that can see the old versions terminate, those old versions need to be removed.
A concept of non-existence that is a central tenet of relational database theory. It represents the absence of a definite value.
The ability to handle parts of executing a query to take advantage of parallel processes on servers with multiple CPUs.

One of several disjoint (not overlapping) subsets of a larger set. In reference to a partitioned table: One of the tables that each contain part of the data of the partitioned table, which is said to be the parent. The partition is itself a table, so it can also be queried directly; at the same time, a partition can sometimes be a partitioned table, allowing hierarchies to be created. In reference to a window function in a query, a partition is a user-defined criterion that identifies which neighboring rows of the query's result set can be considered by the function.
A relation that is in semantic terms the same as a table, but whose storage is distributed across several partitions.
The very first process of an instance. It starts and manages the auxiliary processes and creates backend processes on demand.

A special case of a unique constraint defined on a table or other relation that also guarantees that all of the attributes within the primary key do not have null values. As the name implies, there can be only one primary key per table, though it is possible to have multiple unique constraints that also have no null-capable attributes.
When two or more databases are linked via replication, the server that is considered the authoritative source of information is called the primary, also known as a master.

A type of routine. Their distinctive qualities are that they do not return values, and that they are allowed to make transactional statements such as COMMIT and ROLLBACK. They are invoked via the CALL command.
A request sent by a client to a backend, usually to return results or to modify data on the database.
The part of PostgreSQL that is devoted to determining (planning) the most efficient way to execute queries. Also known as query optimizer, optimizer, or simply planner.
A means of restricting data in one relation by a foreign key so that it must have matching data in another relation.

The generic term for all objects in a database that have a name and a list of attributes defined in a specific order. Tables, sequences, views, foreign tables, materialized views, composite types, and indexes are all relations. More generically, a relation is a set of tuples; for example, the result of a query is also a relation. In PostgreSQL, Class is an archaic synonym for relation.

A database that is paired with a primary database and is maintaining a copy of some or all of the primary database's data. The foremost reasons for doing this are to allow for greater access to that data, and to maintain availability of the data in the event that the primary becomes unavailable.

The act of reproducing data on one server onto another server called a replica. This can take the form of physical replication, where all file changes from one server are copied verbatim, or logical replication where a defined subset of data changes are conveyed using a higher-level representation.
A variant of a checkpoint performed on a replica.

A relation transmitted from a backend process to a client upon the completion of an SQL command, usually a SELECT but it can be an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE command if the RETURNING clause is specified. The fact that a result set is a relation means that a query can be used in the definition of another query, becoming a subquery.
A command to prevent access to a named set of database objects for a named list of roles.

A collection of access privileges to the instance. Roles are themselves a privilege that can be granted to other roles. This is often done for convenience or to ensure completeness when multiple users need the same privileges.
A command to undo all of the operations performed since the beginning of a transaction.

A defined set of instructions stored in the database system that can be invoked for execution. A routine can be written in a variety of programming languages. Routines can be functions (including set-returning functions and trigger functions), aggregate functions, and procedures. Many routines are already defined within PostgreSQL itself, but user-defined ones can also be added.
A special mark in the sequence of steps in a transaction. Data modifications after this point in time may be reverted to the time of the savepoint.

A schema is a namespace for SQL objects, which all reside in the same database. Each SQL object must reside in exactly one schema. All system-defined SQL objects reside in schema pg_catalog. More generically, the term schema is used to mean all data descriptions (table definitions, constraints, comments, etc.) for a given database or subset thereof.

The SQL command used to request data from a database. Normally, SELECT commands are not expected to modify the database in any way, but it is possible that functions invoked within the query could have side effects that do modify data.
A type of relation that is used to generate values. Typically the generated values are sequential non-repeating numbers. They are commonly used to generate surrogate primary key values.
A computer on which PostgreSQL instances run. The term server denotes real hardware, a container, or a virtual machine. This term is sometimes used to refer to an instance or to a host.
A state that allows a client and a backend to interact, communicating over a connection.

RAM which is used by the processes common to an instance. It mirrors parts of database files, provides a transient area for WAL records, and stores additional common information. Note that shared memory belongs to the complete instance, not to a single database. The largest part of shared memory is known as shared buffers and is used to mirror part of data files, organized into pages. When a page is modified, it is called a dirty page until it is written back to the file system.

Any object that can be created with a CREATE command. Most objects are specific to one database, and are commonly known as local objects. Most local objects reside in a specific schema in their containing database, such as relations (all types), routines (all types), data types, etc. The names of such objects of the same type in the same schema are enforced to be unique. There also exist local objects that do not reside in schemas; some examples are extensions, data type casts, and foreign data wrappers. The names of such objects of the same type are enforced to be unique within the database. Other object types, such as roles, tablespaces, replication origins, subscriptions for logical replication, and databases themselves are not local SQL objects since they exist entirely outside of any specific database; they are called global objects. The names of such objects are enforced to be unique within the whole database cluster.
A series of documents that define the SQL language.

An auxiliary process that replays WAL during crash recovery and in a physical replica. (The name is historical: the startup process was named before replication was implemented; the name refers to its task as it relates to the server startup following a crash.)
As used in this documentation, it is a synonym for database superuser.

A collection of tables which describe the structure of all SQL objects of the instance. The system catalog resides in the schema pg_catalog. These tables contain data in internal representation and are not typically considered useful for user examination; a number of user-friendlier views, also in schema pg_catalog, offer more convenient access to some of that information, while additional tables and views exist in schema information_schema that expose some of the same and additional information as mandated by the SQL standard.

A collection of tuples having a common data structure (the same number of attributes, in the same order, having the same name and type per position). A table is the most common form of relation in PostgreSQL.

A named location on the server file system. All SQL objects which require storage beyond their definition in the system catalog must belong to a single tablespace. Initially, a database cluster contains a single usable tablespace which is used as the default for all SQL objects, called pg_default.

Tables that exist either for the lifetime of a session or a transaction, as specified at the time of creation. The data in them is not visible to other sessions, and is not logged. Temporary tables are often used to store intermediate data for a multi-step operation.
A mechanism by which large attributes of table rows are split and stored in a secondary table, called the TOAST table. Each relation with large attributes has its own TOAST table.

A combination of commands that must act as a single atomic command: they all succeed or all fail as a single unit, and their effects are not visible to other sessions until the transaction is complete, and possibly even later, depending on the isolation level.

The numerical, unique, sequentially-assigned identifier that each transaction receives when it first causes a database modification. Frequently abbreviated as xid. When stored on disk, xids are only 32-bits wide, so only approximately four billion write transaction IDs can be generated; to permit the system to run for longer than that, epochs are used, also 32 bits wide. When the counter reaches the maximum xid value, it starts over at 3 (values under that are reserved) and the epoch value is incremented by one. In some contexts, the epoch and xid values are considered together as a single 64-bit value.
Average number of transactions that are executed per second, totaled across all sessions active for a measured run. This is used as a measure of the performance characteristics of an instance.

A function which can be defined to execute whenever a certain operation (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) is applied to a relation. A trigger executes within the same transaction as the statement which invoked it, and if the function fails, then the invoking statement also fails.

A collection of attributes in a fixed order. That order may be defined by the table (or other relation) where the tuple is contained, in which case the tuple is often called a row. It may also be defined by the structure of a result set, in which case it is sometimes called a record.

A type of constraint defined on a relation which restricts the values allowed in one or a combination of columns so that each value or combination of values can only appear once in the relation — that is, no other row in the relation contains values that are equal to those. Because null values are not considered equal to each other, multiple rows with null values are allowed to exist without violating the unique constraint.

The property of certain relations that the changes to them are not reflected in the WAL. This disables replication and crash recovery for these relations. The primary use of unlogged tables is for storing transient work data that must be shared across processes. Temporary tables are always unlogged.
An SQL command used to modify rows that may already exist in a specified table. It cannot create or remove rows.
A role that has the login privilege.
The translation of login credentials in the local database to credentials in a remote data system defined by a foreign data wrapper.
Universal Coordinated Time, the primary global time reference, approximately the time prevailing at the zero meridian of longitude. Often but inaccurately referred to as GMT (Greenwich Mean Time).

The process of removing outdated tuple versions from tables or materialized views, and other closely related processing required by PostgreSQL's implementation of MVCC. This can be initiated through the use of the VACUUM command, but can also be handled automatically via autovacuum processes.

A relation that is defined by a SELECT statement, but has no storage of its own. Any time a query references a view, the definition of the view is substituted into the query as if the user had typed it as a subquery instead of the name of the view.

A storage structure that keeps metadata about each data page of a table's main fork. The visibility map entry for each page stores two bits: the first one (all-visible) indicates that all tuples in the page are visible to all transactions. The second one (all-frozen) indicates that all tuples in the page are marked frozen.
An auxiliary process which, if enabled, saves copies of WAL files for the purpose of creating backups or keeping replicas current.

Also known as WAL segment or WAL segment file. Each of the sequentially-numbered files that provide storage space for WAL. The files are all of the same predefined size and are written in sequential order, interspersing changes as they occur in multiple simultaneous sessions. If the system crashes, the files are read in order, and each of the changes is replayed to restore the system to the state it was in before the crash. Each WAL file can be released after a checkpoint writes all the changes in it to the corresponding data files. Releasing the file can be done either by deleting it, or by changing its name so that it will be used in the future, which is called recycling.

A low-level description of an individual data change. It contains sufficient information for the data change to be re-executed (replayed) in case a system failure causes the change to be lost. WAL records use a non-printable binary format.
An auxiliary process that runs on a replica to receive WAL from the primary server for replay by the startup process.
A special backend process that streams WAL over a network. The receiving end can be a WAL receiver in a replica, pg_receivewal, or any other client program that speaks the replication protocol.
An auxiliary process that summarizes WAL data for incremental backups.
An auxiliary process that writes WAL records from shared memory to WAL files.

A type of function used in a query that applies to a partition of the query's result set; the function's result is based on values found in rows of the same partition or frame. All aggregate functions can be used as window functions, but window functions can also be used to, for example, give ranks to each of the rows in the partition. Also known as analytic functions.
The journal that keeps track of the changes in the database cluster as user- and system-invoked operations take place. It comprises many individual WAL records written sequentially to WAL files.
